group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 59-year-old man arrived to the emergency department in the early hours of Monday morning after taking a rideshare from his apartment because he had developed a fever, productive cough, and right-sided chest tightness that worsened whenever he took a deep breath or climbed the three flights of stairs to his door; he purposefully skipped all morning medications so staff could see his untreated physiology and did not use his home albuterol inhaler or the portable oxygen concentrator that had once been prescribed for a bout of influenza two winters ago. His medical record documents a decade-long history of systolic cardiac dysfunction attributed to a silent myocardial infarction—last outpatient echocardiogram six months earlier showed an ejection fraction of 28 %—for which he ordinarily takes carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, low-dose sacubitril-valsartan, and torsemide 20 mg every morning, though he admits he occasionally forgets the afternoon doses when working late as a city transit dispatcher. He has never required dialysis, carries no diagnosis of chronic kidney impairment, and routine comprehensive metabolic panels at primary-care visits have shown creatinine values near 1.0 mg/dL with no albuminuria. He denies liver disorders, malignancy, prior stroke, or residence in an institutional care setting. Vaccination records captured in the statewide registry confirm the 13-valent pneumococcal conjugate series three years ago and the current season’s inactivated influenza injection. He quit a 15-pack-year cigarette habit seven years prior, limits alcohol to one glass of wine at family dinners, and denies recreational drug use. On arrival he sat upright on the stretcher, conversed coherently, answered the date and current president correctly, and followed a two-step command without hesitation. Untreated triage vitals on room air at this sea-level facility were: oral temperature 38.2 °C, regular tachycardic pulse 106 beats per minute confirmed on telemetry, automated right-arm blood pressure 118/66 mm Hg verified manually, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute with mildly increased thoracoabdominal excursions, and pulse oximetry 91 % without supplemental oxygen. Jugular venous contour remained 4 cm above the sternal angle while he reclined at 45°, similar to the cardiology clinic note from spring, and there was trace pitting edema over both ankles—baseline for him. Heart sounds revealed a quiet third component but no new murmurs or pericardial rub. Pulmonary examination demonstrated decremented breath sounds and dullness to percussion over the right lower one-third of the posterior thorax with a faint bronchial quality just above that zone; inspiratory crackles were scattered in the adjacent parenchyma, and the left lung field remained resonant with vesicular airflow. The abdomen was scaphoid, soft, and nontender with active bowel sounds; no hepatosplenomegaly or ascites was appreciated. Neurologic screen showed equal reactive pupils, intact gaze, symmetric smiles, full grip strength bilaterally, and brisk plantar flexion, without asterixis or confusion. Capillary glucose obtained before venipuncture measured 110 mg/dL. Peripheral venous blood and a left radial arterial sample were drawn within ten minutes of presentation, prior to any saline flushes or medication administration. Chemistry panel revealed sodium 136 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, chloride 100 mEq/L, bicarbonate 24 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 20 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.1 mg/dL. Complete blood count showed leukocytes 13.1 × 10⁹/L with 87 % neutrophils, hematocrit 39 %, hemoglobin 12.7 g/dL, and platelets 260 × 10⁹/L. Arterial blood gas while he continued to breathe ambient air demonstrated pH 7.40, PaCO₂ 40 mm Hg, PaO₂ 68 mm Hg, and calculated bicarbonate 24 mEq/L. Serum lactate returned at 1.7 mmol/L, and high-sensitivity troponin was below the assay threshold. A portable posterior-anterior chest radiograph obtained before any therapy revealed a homogenous opacity filling the right lower lobe with a blunted costophrenic angle and a gently concave upper border consistent with free fluid layering, while cardiomediastinal silhouette was unchanged from the film six months earlier. A brief bedside thoracic ultrasound confirmed an anechoic stripe measuring approximately 3 cm in depth over the right lung base with dynamic air bronchograms in adjacent consolidated parenchyma. Twelve-lead electrocardiography showed sinus tachycardia with low-voltage QRS complexes and nonspecific ST-T changes identical to a tracing on file, without acute ischemia. Two sets of peripheral blood cultures, expectorated sputum for Gram stain and culture, urinary antigens for Legionella pneumophila and Streptococcus pneumoniae, and a respiratory viral PCR panel were dispatched to the laboratory before any antimicrobial, diuretic, bronchodilator, antipyretic, vasopressor, or supplemental oxygen order was placed. To this point the patient has received no medications or intravenous fluids other than minimal heparinized saline to maintain arterial catheter patency, so all physiologic data, laboratory results, and imaging findings described above represent his unaltered presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) sums demographic, comorbidity, examination, laboratory, and radiographic points at presentation.
- Demographics: a man scores his age in years, so age 59 gives 59 points. No nursing-home residence: 0.
- Comorbidities: systolic heart failure (EF 28%) gives 10 points. No malignancy, liver disease, cerebrovascular disease, or chronic renal disease: 0 each.
- Examination: mental status is normal; respiratory rate 24/min is <30; systolic pressure 118 mm Hg is ≥90; temperature 38.2 °C is neither <35 nor ≥40; pulse 106/min is <125. Each scores 0.
- Laboratory findings: arterial pH 7.40 (≥7.35), BUN 20 mg/dL (<30), sodium 136 mEq/L (≥130), glucose 110 mg/dL (<250), and hematocrit 39% (≥30%) each score 0. Room-air PaO₂ 68 mm Hg (≥60) and saturation 91% (≥90%) give 0 oxygenation points.
- Imaging confirms a right pleural effusion: 10 points.
Total = 59 + 10 + 10 = 79 (risk class III).
Final answer: 79
